extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, EPO/UPC practitioners, in-house IP counsel and other stakeholders in European patent practice
extracted.subtask_description: Summary of the EBA decision G 1/24 setting principles for interpreting patent claims when assessing patentability under the EPC, including the role of the description and drawings and the appropriate response to unclear claim language. Targets European prosecution and opposition practice and harmonisation with UPC case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims are the starting point and basis for assessing patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: It is settled case law before the EPO that the claims are always the starting point and the basis for assessing the patentability of an invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing novelty, inventive step, etc., begin with the claim language. However, starting with the claims does not exclude consulting the description and drawings; the claims remain central but are to be interpreted in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description and drawings must always be consulted when interpreting claims
rubrics_metrics.description: “The description and any drawings are always referred to when interpreting the claims, and not just in the case of unclarity or ambiguity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a decisive EBA holding rejecting approaches that limit reference to specification only where claims are unclear. Practitioners and examiners should therefore treat the specification as an integral explanatory aid in every claim interpretation exercise (e.g., the Court endorsed consulting the patent’s explicit definition of “gathered” when interpreting that claim term).

rubrics_metrics.name: There is no single clear EPC article that supplies the legal basis for claim interpretation in assessing patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: The EBA considered that neither Article 69 EPC nor Article 84 EPC are entirely satisfactory as a basis for claim interpretation when assessing patentability and stated that there is no clear legal basis in the EPC articles for claim interpretation in this context (formal answer to Question 1: 'No').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite the absence of a single article, established principles (whether derived from Article 69 or 84) remain applicable; practitioners should not attempt to invent new principles but apply coherent interpretative principles informed by case law and harmonisation considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions in the description should not be disregarded when interpreting claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a term is explicitly defined in the description, that definition is part of the specification context to be considered for claim interpretation and may not be lightly set aside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although Question 3 was held inadmissible as a separate question, amici curiae predominantly argued that explicit definitions in the description should not be disregarded and the EBA’s overall holding that the description is always referred to supports treating such definitions as relevant explanatory material when construing claims (consistent with UPC practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject the 'classical approach' that forbids consulting the description if a term has a clear meaning in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: The Opposition Division’s 'classical approach'—that a term with a clear meaning in the art need not be read against the description—was explicitly rejected by the EBA in G 1/24.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where a term appears clear to the person skilled in the art, examiners, opponents and courts should still take the description/drawings into account rather than automatically excluding them from interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: If a claim is unclear, the correct procedural response is amendment under Article 84 EPC
rubrics_metrics.description: “The correct response to any unclarity in a claim is amendment.” The EBA highlighted the importance of examining divisions carrying out high-quality examinations of clarity under Article 84 EPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where ambiguity or lack of clarity is identified, the appropriate remedy in prosecution is to require amendment of the claim rather than attempting to construe around the ambiguity. This reinforces examiners’ duty to scrutinise clarity during examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonisation with UPC and national courts is a guiding objective for claim interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The EBA emphasised that aligning EPO practice with the practice of national courts of the EPC contracting states and the UPC is desirable and influenced its conclusion that the description/drawings should always be used as explanatory aids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When developing arguments or forming practice, practitioners should be aware of UPC case law (for example NanoString v 10x Genomics) and national courts’ approaches, because the EPO will take harmonisation considerations into account in claim interpretation.
